analogy.p: A smoke detector (receptor) senses smoke and sends a signal along wires (sensory neurone) to a control box (the spinal cord). The control box instantly triggers the sprinklers (effector) through another wire (motor neurone) without waiting for the manager (the brain) to decide; the manager is told afterwards. It breaks down because wires carry the signal electrically all the way, whereas neurones switch to chemical signals at every synapse.
analogy.t: A reflex arc is like a fire alarm

bullets: **Stimulus** = a change in the environment that is detected, e.g. a bright light, a hot surface, a loud noise, a smell, a change in pressure.
**Receptor** = a cell or group of cells that **detects a stimulus** and converts it into an electrical impulse.
**Coordinator** = the **central nervous system (CNS)**, which receives information from receptors, processes it and coordinates the response.
**Effector** = a muscle or a gland that **carries out the response**: muscles **contract**, glands **secrete (release) hormones** or other chemicals.
The chain to learn: **stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → CNS (coordinator) → motor neurone → effector → response**.
Information travels along neurones as **electrical impulses**; between neurones it crosses gaps (synapses) as **chemicals**.
The nervous system is quick because impulses travel rapidly along neurones, so the response starts almost immediately and usually ends quickly.
core.h: The big idea: detect, coordinate, respond
core.p: The nervous system lets humans **react to their surroundings** and **coordinate their behaviour**. A change in the environment (a **stimulus**) is detected, the information is sent as electrical impulses to a processing centre, and that centre sends instructions to a part of the body that carries out a **response**. This happens in fractions of a second, which is why the nervous system is used for fast, short-lived responses (unlike hormones, which are slower and longer-lasting). Almost every exam question on this topic is really asking you to follow the same chain in the right order.

bullets: CNS = **brain + spinal cord**. Do not include the nerves in the CNS; nerves are the 'cables' that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.
The CNS **coordinates** responses; it is the middle step in every response chain.
The **spinal cord** carries impulses between the body and the brain, and is the coordinating centre for many **reflexes**.
The **brain** is involved in voluntary (conscious) actions, memory, learning and processing complex information from the senses.
Bundles of neurones outside the CNS form **nerves**, which carry impulses to and from the CNS.
Damage to the spinal cord can stop impulses passing, causing loss of sensation and/or movement below the injury; this shows how important the cord is as a pathway.
Link to other topics: the CNS works with the **endocrine system** (hormones) to maintain homeostasis.
core.p: The CNS consists of the **brain and the spinal cord**. It is the **coordinator**: it receives impulses from receptors, decides (or automatically produces) the right response, and sends impulses out to effectors. The spinal cord is protected by the backbone (vertebrae) and runs down the back; neurones enter and leave it in pairs at each level of the body. The brain handles conscious thought, memory and complex decisions, whereas the spinal cord can coordinate simple, automatic responses on its own.

bullets: Receptors **convert** the energy of a stimulus (light, pressure, chemicals, temperature) into **electrical impulses**.
**Light receptors** in the retina of the eye detect light; **sound receptors** in the cochlea of the ear detect vibrations; touch, pressure, pain and temperature receptors are in the skin.
**Taste receptors** on the tongue and **smell receptors** in the nose detect chemicals.
Sense organs are organs containing groups of receptors, e.g. eye (light), ear (sound and balance), skin (touch, temperature, pain), tongue (taste), nose (smell).
The sense organ detects the stimulus; the **sensory neurone** carries the impulse; the **CNS** interprets it.
Example exam wording: 'The receptors in the skin detect the heat stimulus and send electrical impulses along sensory neurones to the CNS.'
core.p: A **receptor** is a cell (or group of cells) that detects a specific type of stimulus. Different receptors are sensitive to different stimuli, which is why you can tell light from sound from touch. Receptors are often grouped together in **sense organs**, such as the eye or the skin. When a receptor is stimulated it produces an electrical impulse that starts in a **sensory neurone**. Because each type of receptor detects only its own kind of stimulus, the CNS can work out what has happened from which neurone sent the impulse.

bullets: **Sensory neurone**: receptor → CNS. Carries information **about the stimulus**.
**Relay neurone**: located **within the CNS** (e.g. the spinal cord); links the sensory neurone to the motor neurone.
**Motor neurone**: CNS → effector (muscle or gland). Carries the **instruction** to respond.
Neurones are long and thin (some are over a metre long), so impulses can travel long distances quickly; this is an example of structure matching function.
Neurones are **adapted** to carry electrical impulses; they are covered by a fatty (myelin) sheath in many cases, which speeds up transmission (extra detail, not required by the spec).
A single reflex pathway always uses the same order of neurones: **sensory → relay → motor**.
Between two neurones there is always a tiny gap called a **synapse**.
core.p: Information is carried by cells called **neurones (nerve cells)**. There are three types, defined by what they connect. A **sensory neurone** carries impulses **from receptors to the CNS**. A **relay neurone** is found **inside the CNS** and connects sensory neurones to motor neurones. A **motor neurone** carries impulses **from the CNS to effectors**. Remembering the direction of travel (in to the CNS, across the CNS, out to the body) lets you place each neurone correctly in any diagram.

bullets: **1. Stimulus**: e.g. the hand touches a hot object.
**2. Receptor**: pain/temperature receptors in the skin detect the stimulus and generate an electrical impulse.
**3. Sensory neurone**: carries the impulse from the receptor to the CNS (spinal cord).
**4. Relay neurone**: in the spinal cord, the impulse passes across a **synapse** from the sensory neurone to a relay neurone.
**5. Motor neurone**: the impulse passes across a second synapse to a motor neurone, which carries it out of the CNS.
**6. Effector**: the impulse reaches a muscle (e.g. in the arm), which **contracts**.
**7. Response**: the hand is pulled away from the hot object.
Information about the pain is also sent on to the brain, so you become aware of it **after** the reflex has already happened.
core.h: The reflex arc step by step
core.p: A **reflex action** is an **automatic, rapid response** to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain. The pathway taken by the impulse is the **reflex arc**. Because the impulse does not have to be processed by the conscious brain, the response is much faster, which is essential for protecting the body. Learn the sequence below in order and you can answer any 'describe the pathway' question.

bullets: The electrical impulse arrives at the end of the first (sensory) neurone.
This causes the neurone to **release chemicals** (transmitter substances) into the gap.
The chemicals **diffuse across the synapse** (the gap).
The chemicals **bind to receptor molecules** on the membrane of the next neurone (the relay neurone).
Binding of the chemical **triggers a new electrical impulse** in the next neurone.
Diffusion is **slow over long distances** but fast enough over a tiny gap, so the delay is very small.
Synapses ensure impulses travel in **one direction only**, because the chemicals are released from one side and the receptors are only on the other.
Some drugs and poisons act on synapses, e.g. by blocking receptors or mimicking the chemical (extension idea, not required detail).
core.h: Synapses: how the signal crosses the gap
core.p: A **synapse** is the **junction between two neurones**. There is a tiny gap between them, so the electrical impulse cannot jump directly across. Instead, the impulse is converted into a **chemical signal** for the crossing and then back into an electrical impulse on the other side. This is the standard board explanation and you should be able to write it in order.

bullets: **Automatic**: no conscious decision is required.
**Rapid**: fewer neurones and synapses, and no conscious processing, so a very short delay between stimulus and response.
**Protective**: they help avoid injury, e.g. pulling a hand away from a hot surface, or blinking when something approaches the eye.
Other examples: the **pupil reflex** (pupils get smaller in bright light), the **knee-jerk** reflex when the tendon is tapped, and withdrawing a foot from a sharp object.
Reflexes are not controlled by conscious thought but you can sometimes override them with practice or training (e.g. holding on to a hot plate you are carrying).
Always link the speed of a reflex to the **short pathway** and the **lack of conscious thought**.
core.h: Why reflexes are fast and protective
core.p: Reflex actions are **automatic** (you do not choose them) and **rapid** (they happen quickly). They are fast because the impulse takes a **short route**: the relay neurone in the spinal cord connects directly to the motor neurone, so the information does not have to travel to the brain and be thought about first. The speed means that the body can act to **protect itself from harm** before the damage becomes serious. Reflexes are also inborn (not learned), the same every time, and they do not need conscious thought.

bullets: Reflex pathway: receptor → sensory neurone → **relay neurone (in spinal cord)** → motor neurone → effector.
Voluntary pathway: receptor → sensory neurone → **brain (conscious decision)** → motor neurone → effector.
Reflex: **fast, automatic, involuntary, protective**, not learned.
Voluntary: **slower**, involves thinking, can be changed or learned (e.g. riding a bike).
Both use the same types of neurones and the same stimulus-response structure.
Reaction time (the time between stimulus and response) is shorter for reflexes than for voluntary responses.
The brain still receives information about a reflex afterwards, which is why you feel pain and can learn from it.
core.p: A **voluntary action** involves a conscious decision made in the brain, so the pathway is longer and the response is slower than a reflex. A reflex bypasses the conscious brain. Comparing the two is a favourite 'compare' or 'explain' question, and the key marking points are the route taken, the speed and whether the action is conscious.

bullets: **Muscle effector** → response is **contraction** (the muscle shortens), e.g. biceps contracting to bend the arm.
**Gland effector** → response is **secretion of hormones** or other chemicals, e.g. salivary glands releasing saliva when food is smelt.
Muscles work in pairs (antagonistic muscles); one contracts while the other relaxes (extension knowledge).
In a reflex arc the motor neurone connects the CNS directly to the effector.
Link to endocrine system: a gland effector can release a hormone into the blood, producing a slower, longer-lasting response.
core.p: An **effector** is the part of the body that **produces the response**. In the nervous system there are two types. **Muscles** respond by **contracting**, producing movement (for example pulling the hand away). **Glands** respond by **secreting (releasing) chemical substances**, such as hormones. The response depends entirely on which effector the motor neurone is connected to, which is why the same type of impulse can cause very different responses.

bullets: Nervous: **electrical impulses** (with chemical transmission at synapses); Hormonal: **chemical hormones** in the **blood**.
Nervous: response is **very fast**; Hormonal: **slower**, because hormones must travel in the blood.
Nervous: effect is **short-lived**; Hormonal: effect **lasts longer**.
Nervous: acts on a **precise** target (a specific muscle or gland); Hormonal: acts on **target organs** that have the right receptors, and can affect many cells.
Nervous example: reflex action; Hormonal example: adrenaline released in a frightening situation.
A gland (effector) can be activated by the nervous system, linking the two systems.
core.p: Both the nervous system and the endocrine system coordinate responses, but they work differently. The nervous system uses **electrical impulses** along neurones and gives a **fast, short-lived, precise** response. The endocrine system uses **hormones** carried in the blood and gives a **slower, longer-lasting, more widespread** response. Knowing this contrast helps with 4-mark comparison questions and with later topics such as homeostasis.

bullets: Step 1: identify the **stimulus** (what changed?).
Step 2: name the **receptor** (which cells detect it?).
Step 3: state the **neurone types in order**: sensory, relay, motor.
Step 4: name the **effector** and say whether it **contracts** (muscle) or **secretes** (gland).
Step 5: describe the **response** and say why it is useful (protection).
Use the words **'impulse'** (electrical) and **'neurone'** (not 'nerve' for single cells).
If a question mentions a cut or damaged part of the pathway, think about which step is lost: damaged sensory neurone = no sensation; damaged motor neurone = no movement.
Remember that every point on the pathway is joined by a synapse where the signal is chemical.
core.h: Putting it all together: interpreting diagrams and unseen contexts
core.p: Exam questions often show a diagram of a reflex arc or describe an unfamiliar situation, such as a person standing on a sharp object or a bright light shone in the eye. Your job is to identify the stimulus, receptor, coordinator and effector, and then describe the sequence using the correct vocabulary. Always trace the arrow of the impulse and label each neurone by its direction relative to the CNS.

exam: Command words: **'Describe'** = state the sequence in order; **'Explain'** = give reasons using 'because' or 'so that'; **'Compare'** = write about both, using words like 'whereas'.
**1 mark** definitions: 'a reflex action is an automatic rapid response that does not involve the conscious brain'; 'effector: muscle or gland'.
**2 marks** (e.g. why a reflex is useful): 'it is fast / rapid (1) so it protects the body from harm (1)'.
**3 marks** (describe the pathway): stimulus detected by receptor (1); impulse along sensory neurone to CNS, relay neurone, motor neurone (1); effector (muscle) contracts / gland secretes (1).
**4 marks** (explain how impulse crosses a synapse): impulse reaches end of neurone; chemicals released; diffuse across the gap; bind to receptors on next neurone and trigger a new impulse.
**6 marks** (compare reflex and voluntary): use a clear structure: pathway, speed, role of the brain, whether conscious, purpose; finish with an example of each.
Always use the exact order **sensory → relay → motor** and name the structures (e.g. spinal cord), not just 'nerve'.
On a labelled reflex arc diagram, check the **direction of arrows** and which side of the CNS each neurone enters or leaves.
If asked about 'the effect of damage', link the damaged part to the specific lost function (sensation vs movement).
Use the word **'impulse'** for electrical signals and **'chemical'** for the synapse; do not mix them.
Link to homeostasis: a question may combine the CNS with hormones (e.g. nervous = fast, short; hormones = slow, long).

mistakes.r: The receptor DETECTS the stimulus. The EFFECTOR carries out the response.
mistakes.w: The receptor is the part that responds / moves.

mistakes.r: Reflexes are fast because the pathway is SHORT and does not involve conscious thought in the brain, not because the impulse speeds up.
mistakes.w: Reflexes are fast because the impulse travels faster.

mistakes.r: At a synapse, chemicals are released, diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors on the next neurone, which triggers a new impulse.
mistakes.w: The impulse goes straight across the gap at a synapse as electricity.

mistakes.r: The CNS is the brain and the SPINAL CORD.
mistakes.w: The CNS is the brain and the nerves.

mistakes.r: A MOTOR neurone carries impulses to the effector; the relay neurone is in the CNS and connects sensory to motor neurones.
mistakes.w: A relay neurone carries impulses to the muscle.

mistakes.r: Reflex actions are coordinated by the spinal cord (CNS) without conscious involvement of the brain.
Muscles contract; glands secrete hormones or other chemicals.
Sensory neurones carry impulses FROM receptors TO the CNS.
mistakes.w: Sensory neurones carry impulses to the muscles.

mistakes.r: A reflex is AUTOMATIC and involuntary; it does not involve conscious decision.
mistakes.w: A reflex is a voluntary action done quickly.

summary: The spec asks you to describe the structure and function of the nervous system (receptors, sensory, relay and motor neurones, CNS and effectors), to explain how a reflex arc works including the synapse, and to explain why reflexes are rapid and protective. It matters because it underpins coordinated responses and later work on homeostasis.

terms.d: A change in the environment that is detected by a receptor.
A cell (or group of cells) that detects a stimulus and produces an electrical impulse.
A muscle or gland that brings about a response to a stimulus.
The part of the body (the CNS) that receives information from receptors and coordinates the response.
The brain and the spinal cord.
A nerve cell that carries information as electrical impulses.
A neurone that carries impulses from a receptor to the CNS.
A neurone in the CNS that connects a sensory neurone to a motor neurone.
A neurone that carries impulses from the CNS to an effector.
A junction between two neurones, where a tiny gap is crossed by chemicals.
An automatic, rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought; it protects the body from harm.
The pathway followed by an impulse in a reflex: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
A response that involves conscious thought, with the decision made by the brain.
The action taken by an effector after a stimulus has been detected.
The signal that travels along a neurone.
A bundle of neurones outside the CNS.

worked.ans: Receptors in the skin detect the heat (stimulus) and send electrical impulses along a sensory neurone to the CNS. The impulse crosses a synapse to a relay neurone in the spinal cord and then to a motor neurone. The motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector, a muscle in the arm, which contracts and pulls the hand away. This is a reflex so no conscious thought is needed, making it rapid and protecting the hand from damage.
worked.q: A person touches a hot pan and pulls their hand away before they feel pain. Explain how the reflex arc produces this response. (4 marks)
steps: Name the stimulus and receptor: heat detected by temperature/pain receptors in the skin.
Sensory neurone carries the impulse to the spinal cord (CNS).
Across a synapse to a relay neurone, then across another synapse to a motor neurone.
Motor neurone carries impulse to the effector (arm muscle), which contracts.

worked.ans: The impulse causes the sensory neurone to release a chemical into the synapse (1). The chemical diffuses across the gap (1) and binds to receptors on the relay neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse (1).
worked.q: Explain how an impulse passes from a sensory neurone to a relay neurone. (3 marks)
steps: Impulse reaches the end of the sensory neurone.
Chemicals are released into the synapse.
Chemicals diffuse across the gap and bind to receptor molecules on the relay neurone, starting a new impulse.

worked.ans: A reflex action is automatic and does not involve the conscious part of the brain, whereas a voluntary action involves a conscious decision made in the brain. The reflex pathway is shorter (receptor, sensory, relay in the spinal cord, motor, effector), so the response is faster, whereas a voluntary action takes longer because the impulse is processed by the brain. Reflexes protect the body from harm, e.g. pulling the hand from a hot object.
worked.q: Compare a reflex action with a voluntary action. (4 marks)
steps: Route: reflex goes via spinal cord relay neurone; voluntary goes via brain.
Conscious: reflex automatic; voluntary conscious decision.
